newsitem.title: SPAIN: IMF's Camdessus urges caution on German rates.
newsitem.headline: IMF's Camdessus urges caution on German rates.

text.p: International Monetary Fund Managing Director Michel Camdessus said in an interview published on Tuesday that the Bundesbank must think calmly when analysing a possible hike in interest rates.

"For now, there are no inflationary effects from the dollar in Europe. Besides, the rise in the dollar favours the European Union," he said in an interview with Spanish financial newspaper Expansion during Camdessus' visit to Santander's Menendez Pelayo university at the start of August. "I suggest calmness".
Camdessus said he did not believe the dollar was overvalued.
"I think it is in an acceptable margin of fluctuation," he said. "The rise in its value has been surprising due to the speed, but it was expected for some time".
On the euro, Camdessus said he did not believe the current weakness in European currencies would pave the way for a weak single currency.
"Unless they do something stupid, which of course is unpredictable, the euro will be a strong currency", he said.

Backing up this belief, Camdessus said the euro would be based on some of the most developed and healthy economies in the world. Furthermore, the European Central Bank will be run by people who have a lot of experience in controlling prices.
However, Camdessus said that while Europe had succeeded in becoming more stable, it lacked the flexibility so vital to compete in the war of globalisation against the United States.
Camdessus said some European governments should follow the example of Spain.

"Spain can serve as an example for certain countries," he said. "For a long time it was said that the cost of reducing the defict and inflation would be jobs. But now its (Spain's) economy that is growing, inflation and the deficit are falling and it is creating jobs".
Camdessus praised the work of the U.S. Federal Reserve in correctly predicting the cycle and appropriately tuning its monetary policy.
"The result is that the U.S. is on the point of eliminating its deficit, has sustained growth and is creating high quality jobs," he said.
Camdessus said the Federal Reserve was a good example for the future European Central Bank.
